cases.name: $depth and $ordinal project the row's own property outside a follow
cases.notes: SEMANTICS §2 (0.13): the recursion intrinsics are metadata only on a follow occurrence; anywhere else the name is an ordinary property read. Before 0.13 the six names read absent everywhere they were not metadata, shadowing the row.

cases.name: $stop, $leaf and $frontier are ordinary properties outside a follow
$key outside entries() reads the row's $key property
cases.notes: §21: `$key` is metadata only in an entry scope. An ordinary row that happens to own a `$key` property exposes it; one without reads absent.

cases.name: intrinsic names inside a nested collect read the nested row's property
cases.query: id, kids: kids collect { id, d: $depth, o: $ordinal } from xs

cases.name: a where on $depth without a follow is an ordinary predicate
cases.notes: The seed/post-walk split of §20 exists only when the query has a `follow`; here `$depth > 2` is a plain property comparison over each row.

cases.name: a where on $depth without a follow: a row lacking the property never matches
a row without such properties still reads absent
cases.query: d: $depth, o: $ordinal, s: $stop, l: $leaf, f: $frontier, k: $key from ys

cases.name: order by $ordinal outside a follow sorts by the property, absent last
cases.notes: Unchanged for rows without the property: absent sorts last (§17). A row that owns a `$ordinal` sorts by it.
cases.query: id values from zs order by $ordinal

cases.name: inside a follow the walk's metadata wins over same-named row properties
cases.notes: Every occurrence carries all five recursion intrinsics, so on a follow occurrence the row's own `$depth`/`$ordinal`/`$stop`/`$leaf`/`$frontier` are unreachable by bare name.
cases.query: id, d: $depth, o: $ordinal, s: $stop, l: $leaf, f: $frontier from tree follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: a where on $depth inside a follow is still a post-walk filter over the metadata
cases.notes: The root row's own `$depth` is 99, but the occurrence's `$depth` is 1, so it is filtered out.
cases.query: id values from tree where $depth > 1 follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: inside a nested block within a follow, $depth is the nested row's property and ^$depth the occurrence's
cases.notes: §20: the rows of `children collect { … }` are plain children, not occurrences. `a` owns a `$depth` of 42, so the nested `$depth` reads it; `^$depth` is the occurrence's depth as before.
cases.query: id, kids: children collect { id, own: $depth, occ: ^$depth } from tree follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: $key on a walked successor reads the row's property; the seed keeps its entry key
cases.notes: A seed that arrived as an entry carries `$key` as metadata (§21). A walked successor is not an entry, so its `$key` is an ordinary property read: `L1` owns one, `L2` does not.
cases.query: id, k: $key from entries(forest) follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: an entry scope's $key wins over a $key property of the value
$it is always the scope's row, never a property of it
cases.notes: Step 1 of §2 is unconditional; only steps 2 and 3 fall through to the row. A row property literally named `$it` is shadowed by the intrinsic.

cases.name: $value is an ordinary property: present on the row it projects, absent otherwise
cases.notes: 0.15: the current item is `$it`; `$value` has no intrinsic meaning (and no synonym role). It is a step-5 property read like `$depth` outside a follow.

cases.name: $value values projects the property, null where the row lacks it
$value over scalars is absent, never the scalar
cases.notes: Before 0.15 this read the elements themselves. Navigating a scalar for a property yields absent (§2).

cases.name: $value inside a nested block reads the nested row's own property
cases.query: id, kids: kids collect { id, v: $value, pv: ^$value } from xs

cases.name: $value in an entries() scope is a property of the entry's value, never the entry
cases.notes: §21: the scope's row is the property's value, so `$value` reads the value's own `$value` key. The `{ key, value }` record is the shape of `entries(x)` as a plain VALUE; inside the scope neither `value` nor `$value` names the entry's value — `$it` does.
cases.query: k: $key, v: $value, w: value, it: $it from entries(o)

cases.name: ^$it inside a nested block is the enclosing row
cases.query: id, kids: kids collect { k: $it, parent: ^$it.id } from xs

cases.name: $it values over scalars
cases.query: $it values from xs where $it > 1 order by $it

cases.name: $it.field navigates the row
$it in an entries() scope is the entry's value
$it as a follow by identity
cases.notes: `by $it` keys the walk by the whole row. The two successors share an `id` (the default identity would collapse them within the step) but differ structurally, so both are reached.
cases.query: id, tag from tree follow children { by $it } order by $depth, tag

cases.name: the default follow identity collapses same-id successors where by $it keeps them
cases.query: id, tag from tree follow children order by $depth, tag

cases.name: select $it from scalars keys by its own name
at the root scope an intrinsic name is a named root
cases.notes: Step 5 of §2 at the root: the root scope has no row, so the fall-through is the named root, exactly as for any other bare identifier.
